body:
Merchants Performed Different Functions

Gujarat's overseas trade was organised by people carrying out different commercial activities. Some merchants purchased goods from producers and sold them in wholesale markets. Others financed purchases, owned ships, arranged transport or represented buyers from distant markets.

A successful trading network therefore required more than buyers and sellers. It also needed transport workers, brokers, moneychangers, bankers, sailors and people who managed warehouses and commercial records.

Important Gujarati Merchant Communities

Hindu Baniyas and Jain merchants were prominent in Gujarat's commercial life. They were active in trade, finance and the purchase and distribution of goods.

Muslim Bohra merchants were also important, especially in Surat's maritime commerce. Some wealthy Muslim merchants owned ships and conducted overseas trade.

Surat's trading society was not limited to these communities. Merchants of other regional and religious backgrounds participated in trade. Parsis also served as commercial intermediaries, including as brokers for European trading establishments.

A merchant community was not identical to a single occupation. A person described as a Baniya or a Bohra could undertake different commercial activities. It would be incorrect to assume that all members of a community were only bankers, only shopkeepers or only shipowners.

Important Merchants: Virji Vora and Mulla Abdul Ghafur

Virji Vora was a prominent Surat merchant and financier of the 17th century. His commercial activities illustrate the importance of wealthy Indian merchants in the trading economy in which European companies operated.

Mulla Abdul Ghafur was a leading Muslim merchant associated with Surat's Bohra commercial community and overseas shipping.

Both names are useful because they demonstrate that major Indian merchants possessed commercial resources and influence during the period of expanding European trade. The arrival of European companies did not immediately eliminate Indian participation in large-scale maritime commerce.

Brokers, Bankers and Shipowners

Commercial roleMain functionDistinction
Wholesale merchantBought and sold goods in quantityDealt in commodities
BrokerConnected buyers and sellersArranged transactions on behalf of others
Shroff or sarrafChanged money and performed banking functionsDealt in money, payments and credit
ShipownerProvided or controlled vessels for sea transportDealt with maritime carriage

A merchant could perform more than one of these functions. For example, a wealthy merchant might own goods, finance another trader and possess an interest in shipping.

Caravans and Merchant Associations

Merchants travelling overland often joined caravans to improve security and organise the movement of goods. A caravan was primarily a travelling group.

Merchant associations and guilds served a different purpose: they could represent the interests of members, maintain commercial relationships and help organise trade. Such associations existed in several regions of India, although their names and structures varied.

The terms seth and mahajan are associated with wealthy merchants and established commercial interests. Their precise meaning depends on context. A mahajan could be an influential merchant or moneylender, while the term could also be used in connection with merchant organisations.

Prelims focus

  • Hindu Baniyas, Jain merchants and Muslim Bohras participated in Gujarat's trade.
  • Virji Vora was an important Surat merchant and financier.
  • Mulla Abdul Ghafur was associated with Surat's Bohra merchants and maritime trade.
  • A shroff or sarraf performed moneychanging and banking functions.
  • A caravan was a travelling group; a merchant association was a more continuing commercial organisation.
  • Trap: European trading companies did not create Gujarat's merchant communities; Indian trading networks already existed.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'Traders Big and Small', 'A Gateway to the West: Surat' and 'New Towns and Traders', pp. 79–80 and 84–86; IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, section 29.2.3, p. 24, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Merchant Communities, Shipowners and Trading Organisations in Gujarat

body:
Why Long-Distance Trade Needed Banking

Merchants operating between distant markets had to pay suppliers, receive payments from buyers and finance the movement of goods. Carrying large amounts of coins overland created risks of theft, loss and transport difficulty.

Commercial banking helped merchants transfer funds and obtain credit without relying exclusively on the physical movement of money. Gujarat's trading centres, particularly Surat, were associated with extensive banking and moneychanging activity.

What Was a Hundi?

Hundi

A hundi was a traditional written financial instrument used in commercial transactions. Depending on its form, it could serve as a means of transferring funds, obtaining credit or arranging payment for goods.

In a common remittance arrangement, a merchant could deposit money with a banker in one place and obtain a written instrument enabling payment through a connected banker or agent in another place.

The exact terms depended on the type of hundi and the agreement between the parties. Some hundis were payable on presentation, while others involved payment after a specified period.

How a Remittance Hundi Could Work

Consider a merchant who has received money in Surat but needs to pay a supplier in Agra. Instead of carrying all the coins along the road, the merchant may use a banker with a trusted commercial connection in Agra.

  1. The merchant deposits the agreed sum with a banker in Surat.
  2. The banker issues a hundi directing or providing for payment through a connected banker or agent in Agra.
  3. The instrument is presented to the appropriate party in Agra.
  4. Payment is made according to the hundi's terms and the parties' commercial arrangement.

This is an illustrative remittance transaction. It explains the principle and should not be treated as the compulsory procedure for every type of historical hundi.

Shroffs and the Banking Houses of Surat

A shroff, also called a sarraf, was a moneychanger and financial intermediary who could undertake banking activities. Such work included exchanging coins, handling payments and providing commercial credit.

Surat had wealthy banking houses associated with established merchants and moneychangers. The city's commercial reputation extended well beyond Gujarat.

Surat hundis were recognised in distant trading markets, including Cairo in Egypt, Basra in Iraq and Antwerp in Belgium. This illustrates the reach of the commercial relationships supporting payment and credit.

Credit and Remittance Were Related but Different

FunctionMeaningCommercial purpose
RemittanceTransfer of funds between placesPaying a distant supplier
CreditFunds or purchasing power made available with an obligation to repayFinancing trade before sale proceeds arrive
MoneychangingExchange or valuation of different coinsFacilitating payments made in different currencies

A hundi was not simply another name for a coin or a modern government-issued banknote. Its usefulness depended on accepted commercial practices, the terms of the instrument and confidence in the parties expected to honour it.

Prelims focus

  • A hundi was a traditional financial instrument used for remittance, credit and trade payments.
  • Shroffs or sarrafs were associated with moneychanging and banking.
  • Surat was an important centre of merchant banking.
  • Surat hundis were recognised in Cairo, Basra and Antwerp.
  • Trap: A hundi was a written financial instrument, not the same as physically transporting coins.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'A Gateway to the West: Surat', pp. 84–85; Reserve Bank of India, 'Evolution of Payment Systems in India', Ch. II, sections 2.1 and 2.5–2.8, published 12 December 1998, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A Surat merchant deposits money, receives a hundi, and uses a connected banker in Agra to pay a supplier under its terms.
pictures.caption: A hundi could enable payment between distant markets without transporting the entire amount in coins.

title: Hundis, Shroffs and Banking in Medieval Gujarat's Trade

body:
Why Textiles Were Central to Trade

Textiles were among the important goods exported through Gujarat's ports. Western India, particularly Gujarat and neighbouring regions, was a major centre of textile production. Cloth made in different towns and villages entered regional markets and could then be transported to ports such as Cambay and Surat.

The commercial importance of cloth rested on both its production and its marketability. A merchant needed reliable supplies of fabrics suited to the requirements of buyers in different regions.

The Main Textile Activities

Textile manufacture involved several specialised tasks. The main activities included:

  • Cotton cleaning: Preparing cotton by separating fibres from unwanted material.
  • Spinning: Turning prepared fibres into yarn.
  • Weaving: Interlacing yarn to form cloth.
  • Bleaching: Treating fabric or yarn to remove or reduce unwanted colour.
  • Dyeing: Applying colour to yarn or cloth.
  • Finishing and decoration: Preparing cloth for sale and adding decorative features where required.

These activities could be performed by different craft specialists. The order of bleaching, dyeing and decoration varied according to the material and the desired finished product; not every fabric passed through an identical sequence.

Surat's Zari Textiles

Surat was particularly associated with cotton textiles decorated with zari, including gold-lace borders. Such textiles were valued in markets extending to West Asia, Africa and Europe.

Zari was a decorative feature of certain textiles. It should not be confused with the basic process of growing cotton, spinning yarn or weaving ordinary cloth. Gujarat's trade included different qualities and types of textiles, not only luxury fabrics.

Craft Production and Merchant Orders

Craftspeople produced goods for local markets as well as for distant buyers. Overseas trade expanded the number of potential customers, but artisans often depended on merchants to purchase their products and arrange long-distance sale.

During the period of expanding European company trade, merchants and company agents increasingly used a system of advances. In such an arrangement, a weaver received money before completing the cloth and agreed to supply the promised goods to the purchaser.

This helped buyers secure a supply of cloth, but it could restrict the weaver's freedom to decide where to sell the finished product or which designs to produce. The arrangement did not mean that every Gujarat artisan worked under identical conditions.

The Link Between Crafts and Commercial Prosperity

Growth in textile demand supported work in spinning, weaving, bleaching, dyeing and related activities. Merchants organised purchase and transport, bankers supplied credit and port operators arranged shipping.

The economic connection was therefore direct: inland textile production supplied the goods, while the merchant and maritime networks enabled their long-distance sale.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarat was a major centre within western India's textile-producing region.
  • Cotton cleaning, spinning, weaving, bleaching and dyeing were specialised craft activities.
  • Surat was known for textiles with zari borders.
  • Merchant advances could bind weavers to supplying cloth already promised to buyers.
  • Trap: Zari refers to textile decoration; it is not the name of the port or the financial instrument used in trade.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'Crafts in Towns', 'A Gateway to the West: Surat' and 'New Towns and Traders', pp. 81 and 84–87; NCERT, Craft Traditions of India: Past, Present and Future, Class 11, Ch. 1, 'Crafts in the Past', sections on craft specialisation and textiles, pp. 6–9.]

pictures.caption: Skilled textile workers supplied the cloth that merchants carried to Gujarat's ports.

title: Textile Crafts and Production: The Goods Behind Gujarat's Overseas Trade

body:
Indian Ocean Trade Existed Before European Companies Arrived

Gujarat participated in an Indian Ocean trading system that had developed long before European companies began operating in India. Merchants, sailors and commercial communities connected western Indian ports with markets in West Asia, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China.

Trade moved through several linked ports. Goods might be purchased in one place, carried to another commercial centre and then resold or shipped onwards. This meant that the place from which goods were exported was not always the place where they had originally been produced.

Connections with the Persian Gulf and Red Sea

Surat was especially important for trade with West Asia. Ships sailed towards the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and towards Red Sea markets through the Arabian Sea.

Basra, in present-day Iraq, was an important commercial centre associated with the Persian Gulf trade. Mocha (Mokha) and Jeddah were important Red Sea ports connected with Indian Ocean commercial traffic.

Jeddah was also important for pilgrims travelling towards Mecca. This explains why the same broad maritime connection could support both trade and religious travel.

Connections with East Africa and Southeast Asia

Gujarati merchants also maintained commercial links with the coast of East Africa. Trade connected Gujarat with markets where African commodities, including gold and ivory, entered wider exchange networks.

Routes to Southeast Asia connected merchants with ports around areas such as Sumatra and Java. Trade networks also extended to China. Through these connections, Gujarati markets could obtain products from far beyond the Indian subcontinent.

Major Goods Exchanged

Trade connectionGoods associated with exchangeImportant distinction
Gujarat to overseas marketsTextiles and spicesSome exports were goods assembled through trade rather than produced at the port
East African connectionsGold and ivoryThese entered exchange networks linking Africa and Asian markets
Southeast Asian and Chinese connectionsSpices, tin, Chinese pottery and silverGoods could be redistributed through intermediate ports
Red Sea and Persian Gulf connectionsIndian cloth and other commercial goodsThese routes connected Gujarat with West Asian markets

Textiles and spices are particularly important for understanding Gujarat's export commerce. However, it would be incorrect to assume that every spice shipped through Gujarat was grown there. Merchants could purchase commodities from other producing regions and sell them onwards.

Trade Linked More Than One Region

Commercial relationships were not confined to a simple exchange between India and Europe. Gujarati traders dealt directly or indirectly with merchants in the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China.

European merchants later entered many of these networks, but the underlying connections between Indian and other Asian merchants already existed. European participation altered competition and shipping arrangements rather than beginning Indian Ocean trade from nothing.

Prelims focus

  • The Strait of Hormuz connected Arabian Sea trade with the Persian Gulf.
  • Basra was associated with Persian Gulf commerce.
  • Mocha and Jeddah were important Red Sea ports.
  • Gujarati merchants traded with East Africa, Southeast Asia and China.
  • Textiles and spices were important export goods; African gold and ivory were among goods entering these exchange networks.
  • Trap: The Indian Ocean trading system existed before the arrival of European trading companies.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Ch. 6, 'Traders Big and Small' and 'A Gateway to the West: Surat', pp. 80 and 84; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Ch. 4, 'The Making of a Global World', 'The Pre-modern World', pp. 77–79; IGNOU, Early Modern Cities, Unit 29, section 29.2.2, p. 24, consulted 19 November 2026.]
